nodes.label: employee table
nodes.rationale: One row per person in the office whether or not they log in, so that no signatory or staff record ever refers to a person the system does not know. Holds the identity facts - name parts, position title, org unit, birth date, sex, civil status, tenure status, employment status.

nodes.label: user table (login only)
nodes.rationale: After the split the user row holds only sign-in facts - username, password hash, role_fk, account_status, must_change_password, failed_login_attempts, locked_until, last_login_at - because those are meaningless for a person who never signs in.

nodes.label: employee_fk link on user
nodes.rationale: The link sits on user and is NOT NULL. A login always belongs to a person so the column is never empty there, while on employee it would be empty for most of the office. Required in the database rather than in application code so no code path can skip it and no screen needs a 'no person attached' branch. Confirmed that every account belongs to a real human - no service accounts.

nodes.label: one employee, one login
nodes.rationale: Enforced by the unique constraint user_employee_fk_unique. Two accounts for one human would make 'who changed this record?' ambiguous in the audit history. Different permissions are handled by changing the role, not by a second account.

nodes.label: role_fk stays on the login
nodes.rationale: 'Role' means two things - role in the office (position_title, on employee) and role in the app (a permission bundle, role_fk). On employee the app role would be empty for most of the office and every reader would first have to check whether the person has a login, a check that is easy to forget.

nodes.label: three meanings of 'status' given distinct names
nodes.rationale: employment_status, civil_status, tenure_status on employee and account_status on user. The same word must never be reused for two different things across the two tables, otherwise a later query reads the wrong column. 'separated' unavoidably appears in two of them with different meanings, which is why the column names must stay distinct.

nodes.label: tenure_status (CSC hiring categories)
nodes.rationale: Seven values - permanent, temporary, casual, coterminous, contractual, cos, job_order. COS and Job Order are listed apart because those people are not government employees under Civil Service Commission rules but engaged under a separate joint circular. 'substitute' is excluded because the office never fills a post while its holder is on long leave; coterminous is a different idea, tied to a term or project rather than to an absent person.

nodes.label: employment_status (active / separated)
nodes.rationale: Says whether the person still works here, separate from whether a login is active or locked. Still uncertain whether it needs finer values telling retirement, resignation and end of contract apart.

nodes.label: account_status (renamed from status)
nodes.rationale: active, inactive, locked. Renamed from the plain 'status' column so no word is shared between the two tables.

nodes.label: no employee number column
nodes.rationale: The plantilla item number applies only to regular employees, so the column would be empty for the Contract of Service and Job Order part of the office.

nodes.label: position_title and tenure_status are required
nodes.rationale: The office hires a person into a named position, so a staff record with no position is not a real case; COS and JO staff hold no plantilla item but still hold a position or designation. They were optional at first only because they had been optional on the old user table. Consequence - create-admin.ts must write placeholders ('System Administrator', 'Permanent') and warn to correct the record afterwards.

nodes.label: light HR flavour, not a personnel system
nodes.rationale: Follow Civil Service Commission conventions where they exist so the fields feel familiar, but do not over-build. Leave records, payroll and service records are out of scope - this is an environmental management system.

nodes.label: two admin screens instead of one
nodes.rationale: The combined dialog would ask for fourteen things; the two lists are different sizes (everyone vs only account holders); and the two jobs differ - clerical staff-list upkeep vs deciding who may do what. Accepted drawback - hiring someone who needs a login means visiting two pages. A 'Give this person a login' row action is a possible later improvement, recorded but not decided.

nodes.label: Employees page (/admin/employees)
nodes.rationale: Five columns - Name (with position underneath), Section, Tenure, Employment, Has login. Birthday, sex and civil status are edit-only because nobody scans a staff list for a birthday and they should not sit on screen for passers-by. Built as recommended rather than agreed, still open to change.

nodes.label: Users page (logins only)
nodes.rationale: Adding an account picks somebody already on the Employees page instead of typing a name; people who already have an account stay listed but unpickable so they do not read as missing. The person is locked when editing, because moving a login to another person is a new account, not an edit.

nodes.label: 'Has login' column
nodes.rationale: The one column reaching across to the Users page. It answers the question the separation creates - who in this office still has no account - which would otherwise require opening both pages and comparing by hand.

nodes.label: admin:view_employees and admin:manage_employees
nodes.rationale: A new 'employees' submodule under admin in PERMISSION_DEFS. Kept apart from admin:manage_users because creating a login and assigning a role decides who may do what system-wide, while correcting a spelling or recording a birth date does not. The Users page can still list employee names without admin:view_employees - that key controls opening the page, not reading names elsewhere.

nodes.label: super-admin backfill in the permission sync
nodes.rationale: scripts/sync-permissions.ts had three steps instead of the four the locked RBAC decisions require; re-normalizing does not help because nothing implies admin:manage_employees - implication runs upward only. The super-admin role is frozen and has no UI path to gain a module, so a missing key could only have been fixed by editing role_permission by hand. The added step finds the role by admin:manage_roles rather than by name, inserts what is missing in one transaction, names what it added, and skips gracefully on a fresh database. Staff keys are deliberately excluded.

nodes.label: sign-in refuses anyone no longer employed
nodes.rationale: Option C of three. Chosen over 'also switch the account off' because that leaves a gap - an admin could switch the account back on later without touching the employment record. The rule cannot be forgotten because it lives in the sign-in path. Accepted cost - the Users page must also show that the person has left, otherwise it reads 'Active' for an account that refuses to work.

nodes.label: endSessionsForEmployee
nodes.rationale: Shared helper deleting a person's session rows, called from both the Employees page 'separate' action and from 'update' when an edit is what marks them as having left - the editor was the second way in and would otherwise have left them signed in.

nodes.label: session validation joins employee
nodes.rationale: validateSessionToken in src/lib/server/auth/session.ts inner joins employee (inner because user.employee_fk cannot be null) and deletes rather than merely refuses a session whose employee is not active, so the row does not sit until its eight-hour expiry.

nodes.label: SessionUser with nested employee object
nodes.rationale: Kept nested rather than flattened so it stays visible which table each field came from. hooks.server.ts builds this shape into locals.user, passing only the fields the app displays - birth date, sex and civil status stay on the server.

nodes.label: create-admin.ts two-insert bootstrap
nodes.rationale: Inserts the employee row first, then the login pointing at it, both in one transaction so a taken username does not leave an orphan employee when the prompt retries.

nodes.label: Organizational Structure page reads employee
nodes.rationale: org_unit_fk moved to employee, so the endpoint moved from [org_unit_pk]/users to [org_unit_pk]/employees and filters on employment_status. The delete guard had to move too - checking user would have let a populated division be deleted. Side effect - the list now includes people with no login, which is what the page always meant to show.

nodes.label: shared faceted filter and facet helpers
nodes.rationale: The filter dropdown moved to src/lib/components/faceted-filter.svelte and its counting helpers to src/lib/utils/facets.ts once two tables needed them, rather than being written twice.
